title: Sounding Sure Isn't Evidence
objective: After this level you can explain why a confident, fluent delivery is not a reason to believe a claim.
summary: Confidence persuades because it often goes with knowledge, but it can be sent without any. Style isn't substance, and a bare assertion isn't an argument, however loud.

cards.headline: Two friends give directions. "Left. Definitely." "Um, left, I think?"
cards.body: Which friend do you follow? The sure one sounds more persuasive, and that isn't an accident. This level is about why confidence persuades, and why the way a claim is said can feel like evidence when it isn't.

cards.headline: Why confidence persuades
cards.body: Researchers call the shortcut the confidence heuristic: people are confident when they know they're right, and their confidence makes them persuasive. That's why the shortcut exists. Often the sure-sounding friend really does know the way. The trap is that the signal can be sent without the knowledge behind it. Anyone can say "definitely".

cards.headline: Style isn't a premise
cards.body: The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy lists a fallacy called style over substance: taking the style of an argument as adding to its strength. A salesperson's smile and sharp clothes add nothing to their reasons. Level 2 gave you the rule already: asserting a view, however heatedly, isn't giving an argument. Volume, polish and certainty are how a claim is said, not a reason to believe it.

cards.headline: Sure and wrong
cards.body: In a 2007 study, Elizabeth Tenney and colleagues found that confident witnesses were judged more credible than unconfident ones. But errors damaged the confident witnesses' credibility more. After a mistake, the less confident witness could seem the more believable one. So treat confidence as a claim about knowledge, and check it: ask for the reason, and remember who has been sure and wrong before.

cards.headline: Confidence: weighed
learned: Confidence persuades because it often tracks knowledge
Confident errors cost the most credibility

questions.prompt: In Elizabeth Tenney's 2007 study, whose credibility suffered most after an error?

options.label: Everyone's credibility fell by the same amount

questions.explanation: Errors damaged the credibility of witnesses who had been confident more than that of unconfident ones.

questions.prompt: Why can confidence mislead, even though confident people are often right?

options.label: Confidence always means the speaker is wrong
options.rationale: It often goes with knowledge; that's why it persuades.

options.label: Anyone can sound sure without the knowledge behind it
People never find confidence persuasive
options.rationale: The confidence heuristic says they do.

questions.explanation: Confidence persuades because it often tracks knowledge, but the signal can be sent without the knowledge.

questions.prompt: "Trust me, it's definitely true!" Why is this not an argument, by Level 2's test?

options.label: It uses the word "definitely"
options.rationale: The word isn't the problem; the missing reason is.

options.label: It asserts a view but gives no reason
It's too short to count
options.rationale: Short arguments exist; this one has no premise.

options.label: It's said by a friend
options.rationale: Who says it doesn't matter; there's no reason given.

questions.explanation: Asserting a view, however heatedly or confidently, isn't giving an argument; offering a reason is.
